tier_reason: The README's Performance table is explicitly 'maximum theoretical performance' computed from instruction counts for an unnamed reference system, not a measurement; the IEEE-path eFP64 column is empty and nothing in the repo or the linked openmm-benchmarks/FP64Emulation folder (Trial1.swift, Trial2.swift, Trial3.cl, bing-conversation.md) times a real workload. The 'baseline' is the CPU's hardware FP64 peak, not GMP or MPFR.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'Performance' table of maximum theoretical scalar Gops (not measured), CPU FP64 vs GPU FP32x2 (double-single, 1+47-bit mantissa): FFMA 392 vs 590, FADD 196 vs 482, FMUL 196 vs 758, FCMPSEL 196 vs 2123, FCMP 196 vs 1769, FRECIP 49 vs 196, FDIV 49 vs 183, FRSQRT 49 vs 171, FSQRT 49 vs 189 (ratios 1.5x to 10.8x, derived from page data). The 'GPU eFP64' column (float64_t with edge-case checking disabled) is empty. Text: 'Based on theoretical estimates, additions and multiplications will have 1/32-1/64 the throughput of their 32-bit counterparts.'
corrections.caveats: The README says 'Still in the planning stage - this is not a finished library!'. The only numbers are theoretical peaks from instruction counts (the README's own 'maximum theoretical performance'); no workload was timed anywhere I could open, the eFP64 column (float64_t with edge-case checks disabled) is blank and the precision table is mostly '???'. The comparison is not like-for-like: the CPU column is full IEEE FP64, while the filled GPU column is FP32x2 double-single with an 8-bit exponent and 1+47-bit mantissa that flushes denormals and gives undefined results for INF/NAN. The comparison is against the CPU's hardware double, not the category baselines GMP or MPFR (software arbitrary precision), so the entry does not fit big-integer-arbitrary-precision; it would sit better with floating-point emulation or GPU numerics. The README credits GPT-4 for much of the work. Archived (read-only) on 2024-08-11; last commit 2023-05-17.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly; they are theoretical, so D stands. Wrong category (FP64 emulation on Apple GPUs vs CPU FP64, not arbitrary precision vs GMP/MPFR); 65 stars and tier D would allow a not-notable-tier-d reject, but I confirmed it so the keep-and-document rule applies. Metadata verified: MIT, 65 stars, 3 forks, not a fork, archived 2024-08-11, last commit 2023-05-17 ('Correct for rounding error'), abandoned.

tier_reason: Nothing I could open has numbers: the README says only 'For large tensors reaches peak matrix-times-matrix performance', the wiki home page has no benchmarks, and example/measure.cpp times only TTM's own variants with no Eigen, LibTorch, MKL batched-GEMM or TBLIS run. The peer-reviewed Journal of Computational Science 2025 article (vol. 87, 102568, cited in the README) holds the claimed comparison, but ScienceDirect is egress-blocked here and the record's figures come only from the search agent's search-engine summary, which I could not re-check (WebSearch off-limits for this run).

corrections.caveats: No numbers or baseline comparison in the repository: the README gives only a qualitative claim, the wiki home page has no benchmarks (the other three wiki pages failed to load), and example/measure.cpp (g++ -O3, cache flush between runs) times only TTM's own parallel/slicing/fusion variants. The comparison against Eigen, LibTorch, MKL batched GEMM and TBLIS exists only in the peer-reviewed article 'Design of a high-performance tensor-matrix multiplication with BLAS' (Bassoy, Journal of Computational Science 87, 2025, 102568; doi 10.1016/j.jocs.2025.102568), which neither the search agent nor the verifier could open (ScienceDirect, doi.org, arXiv and tore.tuhh.de are egress-blocked). Every number in claimed_speedup is from one search-engine summary of the abstract and is UNVERIFIED; per that summary the average gain over frameworks is as low as 6.21% and TBLIS is a tie for most shapes. It is the author's own benchmark of his own library; compiler, flags, library versions and whether the benchmark code is public are unknown. The author's GitHub account has no separate artifact repo (only ttm, ttv, tlib, simd, matrix and forks). The README badge says GPL while LICENSE.txt and GitHub show LGPL-3.0. A check that can open the paper should restore B (or A if it names a public artifact with compiler, flags and CPU), as for the sibling bassoy/ttv entry (B, ICCS 2019).

notes: Downgraded B to D because no reachable page shows numbers; do not reject: the peer-reviewed JoCS 2025 article exists (README bibtex) and the sibling bassoy/ttv is already verified at B. tier_reason: The README Performance Results section and its charts (docs/costa-same.svg, docs/costa-diff.svg, rendered here) show first-party pdgemr2d times for COSTA vs MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 on 8 Piz Daint nodes, produced by the public miniapps/pxgemr2d_miniapp.cpp, which runs both COSTA and ScaLAPACK in one binary. No compiler, flags or CPU model is stated, so not A; the peer-reviewed ISC21 paper (Springer LNCS, arXiv 2106.06601) could not be opened, so B is not confirmed.

corrections.caveats: The baseline is MKL's ScaLAPACK redistribution routine pdgemr2d, not a BLAS or LAPACK kernel, so it only loosely fits the blas-lapack baselines. The identical-layout case (about 20x) most likely reflects MKL's slow generic path when no data needs to move (my inference, not stated by the authors). The charts are first-party; MKL and MPI settings, the compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated, and the README does not say which repetition or statistic is plotted (the miniapp's n_rep default is 2 and it prints every repetition's time in ms for both COSTA and ScaLAPACK). The benchmark code is public (miniapps/pxgemr2d_miniapp.cpp, pxtran_miniapp.cpp). The peer-reviewed paper (Kabic, Pintarelli, Kozhevnikov, VandeVondele, ISC 2021, Springer LNCS pp. 217-236; arXiv 2106.06601) is cited in the README but could not be opened (Springer and arXiv are blocked in this session); a check that can open it should consider B and whether its numbers match the README charts. 'Orders of magnitude' in the README overview is not shown by these charts (largest ratio about 21x). Numbers were read from the chart data labels.

notes: All ten COSTA/MKL data labels in the record match the rendered charts exactly, and the derived ratios (19.4x-21.2x same layout, 2.2x-2.9x different layouts) are correct.
